query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior do not improve with increasing Mg content and optimized alloy composition, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study investigated the effects of composition and processing on the microstructure, hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance of spark plasma sintered Mg-Ti-Zn alloys. Key findings include: MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn alloys were produced via ball milling and spark plasma sintering. XRD, SEM, and STEM analyses revealed the presence of multiple phases. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high hardness and stiffness, which were much higher than those of any commercial Mg alloy. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high corrosion resistance (indicated by the high corrosion potential and low corrosion current density) and passivation, which were attributed to the formation of a Ti rich surface film. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining mechanical alloying and SPS to engineer Mg-containing multi-principal element alloys with a rare combination of high hardness and corrosion resistance. This strategy offers a new pathway for designing lightweight structural or biomedical materials that overcome the traditional strength–corrosion trade-off in Mg and Zn alloys. In this work, alloy Nb–30Ti–10Si–5Cr–5Sn–3Fe–2Al–2Hf (NV2) was studied in the as-cast and heat-treated conditions: its isothermal oxidation at three pest oxidation temperatures and its room temperature hardness and specific strength were evaluated and compared with other Sn-containing RM(Nb)ICs—in particular, alloy NV5—and with RCCAs and RHEAs. The issues that motivated this research were resolved. The synergy of Fe with Al, Cr, Hf and Sn (a) stabilised Nbss; A15–Nb3X (X = Al, Si and Sn) and Nb3Si, metastable Nb3Si-m’ and Nb5Si3 silicides; (b) supported the formation of Nbss + Nb5Si3 eutectic in the cast microstructure; (c) suppressed pest oxidation in the temperature range 700–900 °C and (d) stabilised a Cr-rich π phase instead of a C14–Nb(Cr,Fe)2 Laves phase. Furthermore, it was shown that complex concentrated (CC) or high entropy (HE) phases coexisted with “conventional” phases in all conditions and after oxidation at 800 °C.
